```python
def get_digit_sum(n):
    # Ensure n is treated as absolute value since we're interested only in magnitudes.
    abs_n = abs(int(n))

    total = 0

    while(abs_n != 0): 
        remainder_of_division_by_10 = int( (abs_n % 10) )
        total += remainder_of_division_by_10 

        abs_n /= 10;  
        
    return(total)

# Testing your function:
print(get_digit_sum(-2345))   # should print `8`
```

This program works by repeatedly dividing the passed-in argument (`n`) into two parts - one containing all but last decimal place figures from right end(`remainder`), another having just single figure at unit position which will then add up with our running tally variable named 'total'. This process continues until there are no more digits left i.e., when original_number equals zero after division operation .

Assistant: In JavaScript, both `'` (single quotes) and `"` (double quotes) are used to define strings. They serve essentially the same purpose—enclosing text within your code—and can be interchanged freely for defining string literals.

However, there’s one subtle but important distinction when it comes to embedding variables or other values inside these quoted strings:

### Single Quotes (`'`)
- When you use single quotes around a value that contains special characters like apostrophes ('), those must themselves also be enclosed with additional sets of either type if they need escaping:
  ```javascript
    let message = 'She said "Hello!"';
```
Here, `"Hello!"`
is not an issue because we're using different types of delimiters - outer single quote marks contain inner double-quote-delimited content without needing any extra handling via backslashes (\).

#### Double Quotes ("")
Similarly,
```JavaScript 
let greeting = “Good Morning”; // Using escaped character ' instead.
console.log(greeting); //" GoodMorning "
// Alternatively...
let name=“John”;
alert(`Hi ${name} how’re u ?`);
```

In this case too, proper usage dictates wrapping anything potentially containing embedded quotations correctly so as avoid ambiguity during parsing by engine interpreters.

So while technically interchangeable under many circumstances regarding basic syntax rules governing literal contents representation – choosing which pair depends largely upon stylistic preference among developers working collaboratively on projects where consistency matters most!
